The developers recently created a Web site -- iPhoneSIMfree.com -- but there is very little information on it and no direct way for anyone to purchase the software. LOS ANGELES (CNN) -- A group of anonymous software developers announced plans to soon begin selling a program that will enable iPhone owners to use the immensely popular device on cellular networks worldwide, rather than being restricted to AT&T alone.

Apple's iPhone has yet to be released outside the United States. Since its debut in the U.S. two months ago, the device has been engineered to operate exclusively on the AT&T network for its first two years, per an exclusive agreement between Apple and AT&T.

Brett Schulte, a Los Angeles-based software consultant unaffiliated with the developers, demonstrated the software for CNN on Friday evening. Within seconds of Schulte swapping the AT&T SIM card for a T-Mobile one, an iPhone equipped with the new software appeared to function seamlessly on the T-Mobile network.

"It's completely software hacked," Schulte explained. "There's no case opening required. It's not necessary to perform any kind of disassembly." The entire unlocking process took Schulte roughly two minutes to complete.

The developers declined to share their last names with CNN, citing concerns that "we don't want to be hounded." They indicated that sales of the software—whose price has yet to be determined—would begin once their online payment and customer service infrastructure is operational. They are also awaiting further guidance from their legal counsel.

Apple spokeswoman Jennifer Bowcock told CNN that the company had no comment on the matter. AT&T spokesman Mark Siegel declined to speculate on the legality of unlocking the phone, but noted, "When you sign up, you're signing a two-year contract. You're obligated to pay the bill."

"When people buy the iPhone, it's clear from our materials that it's designed to operate exclusively on AT&T," Siegel added.

Schulte countered, however, that it is possible to purchase an iPhone without entering into a contractual obligation with AT&T.

The developers recently launched a website—iPhoneSIMfree.com—though it currently offers minimal information and no direct means of purchasing the software. Internet domain records show the site was registered less than two weeks ago.

Two members of the group, identifying themselves only as "John" and "Liu," told CNN in a phone interview that a core team of six individuals spanning three continents had worked on unlocking the iPhone as a hobby. They described themselves as devoted fans of Apple products who believed the iPhone should be made available to those unable to use AT&T's network.

"I'm not in America, and I can't use it," said Liu, who declined to disclose his country of residence. "It's not fair."

When asked whether he believed modifying the iPhone was legal, he responded, "That's a very good question. I truly believe it is."

John and Liu stated that neither Apple nor AT&T had contacted them thus far, though they acknowledged that circumstances could change the moment their software becomes available for sale.

Earlier this month, a teenager devised his own method for unlocking the iPhone, though his approach required disassembling the device.

A group of anonymous developers is preparing to sell software that will unlock Apple's iPhone, allowing the device to operate on cell phone networks worldwide rather than being confined to AT&T's network in the United States. This development could significantly alter the landscape for iPhone users, particularly those outside the U.S. who have been unable to legally purchase and use the device on their local carriers.

## Background on iPhone's Exclusive Network Arrangement

When Apple launched the iPhone, the company struck an exclusive two-year agreement with AT&T, making it the only carrier in the U.S. authorized to provide service for the device. This arrangement has meant that iPhone owners have had no choice but to use AT&T's network, regardless of their location or preference for other carriers. Compounding this limitation, Apple has yet to release the iPhone internationally, leaving customers in other countries without any official means of obtaining the device altogether—until now, if this unlocking software proves viable.

## Pricing and Launch Details Still Pending

Despite the successful demonstration, the developers behind the software have not yet finalized a price for their product. Before they can begin selling the unlocking tool to the public, they are waiting on two key factors: legal counsel regarding the implications of distributing such software, and the completion of the necessary infrastructure to support sales, including an online payment system and customer service capabilities. What makes this development particularly remarkable is the elegance and simplicity of the hack. Unlike earlier unlocking attempts for other phones that required physical disassembly, soldering, or specialized hardware tools, this iPhone unlock works entirely through software. Users don't need to crack open their devices or void warranties through invasive physical modifications—the entire process can reportedly be accomplished through code alone.

The significance of this breakthrough extends far beyond simple network switching. This arrangement was a cornerstone of the iPhone's launch strategy, and the unlocking software directly circumvents the restrictions built into the device to enforce that exclusivity.

The legal implications remain murky. Questions abound regarding whether creating, distributing, or using such unlocking software violates the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA), breaches terms of service agreements, or potentially exposes users to legal liability from either Apple or AT&T.

Rather than stepping into the spotlight to take credit for their technical achievement, they appear to be exercising caution, seemingly waiting to better understand the legal landscape before revealing their identities. For now, the anonymous developers' creation stands as a testament to the ingenuity of the hacking community and a reminder that exclusivity agreements, no matter how carefully constructed, may only be as strong as the software protecting them.

# Underground Developers Crack iPhone Carrier Lock, Sparking Industry Debate

**TECHNOLOGY DESK** — A group of anonymous programmers has developed and released a software tool that allows Apple's iPhone to operate on wireless networks beyond AT&T, the device's exclusive U.S. carrier partner, raising fresh questions about consumer rights, corporate exclusivity deals, and the limits of device ownership.

The tool, which reportedly circulated through online forums and hacker communities before gaining wider attention, works by unlocking the iPhone's baseband software—the component that ties the device to a specific carrier's network. Once modified, users can allegedly insert SIM cards from other carriers, enabling the phone to send calls, texts, and data over non-AT&T networks.

## A Workaround Years in the Making

Since the iPhone's launch, Apple and AT&T have maintained a tightly controlled exclusivity arrangement, part of a multi-year agreement believed to be worth billions to both companies. Critics have long argued that such lock-in agreements limit consumer choice and inflate costs, particularly for customers who travel internationally or live in regions with poor AT&T coverage.

The anonymous developers, who have not revealed their identities or affiliations, published technical details and, in some cases, downloadable software packages through independent websites. Members of the hacking community describe the effort as part of a broader culture of "jailbreaking"—modifying Apple's tightly controlled software ecosystem to expand device functionality beyond what the company officially sanctions.

## Industry and Legal Reactions

Neither Apple nor AT&T has issued detailed public comment on the specific tool, though both companies have historically maintained that unauthorized modifications void device warranties and may violate terms of service. Legal experts note that unlocking a phone exists in something of a gray area—permissible in some interpretations of copyright and telecommunications law, murky in others.

Consumer advocacy groups have largely welcomed the development. "This is about giving people control over hardware they've purchased," said one telecommunications policy analyst. "If someone owns an iPhone, there's a reasonable argument they should be able to choose their own network."

Carriers outside the AT&T partnership have been notably quiet, neither endorsing the unauthorized use of unlocked iPhones on their networks nor explicitly barring it.

## What Comes Next

Technology observers expect Apple to respond with software updates aimed at closing the loophole, a pattern seen repeatedly in the ongoing back-and-forth between the company and the jailbreaking community. Whether such updates will succeed—or simply spawn a new generation of workarounds—remains an open question.

For now, the anonymous programmers appear to have achieved their stated goal: proving that the iPhone's carrier restrictions are a matter of software policy, not technical necessity. Whether that proof leads to lasting change in how smartphones are sold and locked to carriers is likely to play out over months, if not years, of continued friction between manufacturers, carriers, and the users who buy their devices.

*This story may be updated as more information becomes available.*

---

The exclusivity arrangement that has tied Apple's iPhone to a single wireless carrier appears to be cracking, quite literally, as independent software developers release tools that strip away the phone's carrier restrictions and allow it to run on other networks.

Since the iPhone's debut, it has been locked to work only with AT&T's network in the United States, part of a multiyear exclusivity deal between the two companies. But over the past several days, hobbyist programmers and hacking collectives have published free software that reverses the phone's carrier lock, allowing owners to insert SIM cards from other providers—including networks overseas—and use the device as they see fit.

The unlocking tools spread rapidly across online forums, with tens of thousands of downloads reported within the first 48 hours. Unlike earlier "jailbreak" hacks that merely allowed unauthorized third-party applications, this new class of software goes a step further, targeting the baseband firmware that ties the phone contractually and technically to AT&T.

"This isn't about piracy or theft," said one of the anonymous developers involved in the project, who goes by a handle rather than a real name in online communities. "We bought these phones. We should be able to decide which network they run on."

The unlocking software does not violate copyright law in any traditional sense, according to several technology attorneys, though it may run afoul of terms-of-service agreements signed by purchasers. The U.S. Copyright Office has previously granted exemptions under the Digital Millennium Copyright Act permitting consumers to unlock phones they own for use on other carriers, though the applicability of those exemptions to Apple's specific technology remains untested in court.

Reached for comment, an AT&T spokesperson expressed concern about the implications for customers who attempt the unauthorized modification.

"We want to remind customers that the iPhone was designed and sold as part of an integrated experience with AT&T's network," the spokesperson said. "Modifying the device in ways not authorized by Apple could result in a phone that no longer functions properly, and customers who go this route do so at their own risk. "Every time a company tries to lock down a highly desirable piece of hardware, someone treats it as a puzzle to be solved," said one telecommunications analyst who tracks the wireless industry. "The exclusivity deal between Apple and AT&T was always going to be a target, especially for iPhone owners outside the U.S. who have no legal way to use the phone on their local networks."

Indeed, much of the early enthusiasm for the unlocking software has come from overseas buyers, who purchased iPhones during international trips or through resellers, only to find the devices useless without an AT&T SIM card. For many of them, the unlock represents the first legitimate path to using hardware they already own.

### What Comes Next

For now, the unlocking tools remain freely available, and their user base appears to be growing daily.
